doc.title: Michael Abene interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 11, 2003

title: Pricing arrangements and doing work for love
summary: Abene advises using Local 802 orchestrator scale as a gauge for pricing, and describes taking jobs like Mel Lewis's band for the music.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Managers, bookers and the business of getting work

blocks.x: The skeleton of it all, and then you give it to the orchestrator, and some of these orchestrators you never heard of, who are not only fabulous but that’s also a very lucrative — the only bad part for me would be it’s like being buried under something else you know. So I was never inclined to do that end of it. Over the years you establish a price for yourself basically. And there’s no — a lot of times an arranger starting out, he says well how should I charge? I said well you know what you do? Go to your Local — if you’re in New York go to Local 802, get what the orchestrator’s scale is. Figure out that scale, what it is so at least when you bargain with somebody you have some idea, you know you don’t just pull a number out of the hat. Because the guy will say how did you come to that price? And you say oops. So at least if you know say a chart at scale is $500. So you’re asking $700, all right? So you have some kind of a gauge. So if he says well I can only pay you $150. So now you have to decide, and we’ve all done this, if you want to do that chart. How important is that chart for you to do? To this day, I don’t care who the writer is, there are certain jobs you do that pay more — will pay your price and can afford to. Then there are some situations you really want to do a particular project and they just can’t afford it. It’s a budgetary thing. So you decide, oh it’s not worth it. I don’t want to do it. Or you say well it’s a very important scene, it’s a wonderful orchestra, a wonderful band and there’s other far reaching things. So I mean I really feel that goes on to this day. Like I’ve done stuff for Liza Minelli over the years. So of course you’re talking a whole other thing. Then when I did stuff for Mel Lewis for the Vanguard, now you know there’s quite a difference. But certainly when Mel talked to me about it, sure man, love to do some stuff for the band. We didn’t even talk about money. I mean now you’re talking about something else now.
Yeah, you’re thinking about the people in that band playing your music for one thing.
Yeah. Come on, there’s no comparison. So for somebody to refuse that on the basis of well he’s not paying me X amount, the guy’s in the wrong business.
Right. Certain things you do for the love of it, right?
